title: Action pipelines and runtime guards demo with Nexus Cloud
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood's JSON-mode action pipelines, runtime guardrails, and tool-calling patterns. Focus on schema-enforced outputs, fallback routing, and pilot scope for Nexus Cloud's multi-tenant ingestion use case. Agreed next steps include security pack, pilot SOW and benchmark run.
action_items: Maya Chen: Send SOC2 + security pack and redwood-private architecture note by 2027-05-06
Liam O'Connor: Provide pilot infra estimate (GPU types, expected throughput) and sample batch/quantization profile by 2027-05-08
Amira Rahman: Share representative prompt set and sample documents (anonymized) by 2027-05-07
Daniel Park: Confirm pilot stakeholders and acceptance criteria (latency, cost per 1k tokens) by 2027-05-10
next_steps: Maya to email security artifacts and a sample pilot SOW
Run 1k request baseline benchmark with 512 token context; Redwood to run and share results
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-04 17:30 UTC, Duration 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood PM); Daniel Park (CTO, Nexus Cloud), Amira Rahman (ML Eng), Carlos Mendes (Platform Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Security)
---
Summary: quick walkthrough of JSON-mode action pipelines, show Console flows in Redwood Optimize, discuss privacy options (Dedicated vs Private), and agree pilot scope.
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we've got Daniel, Amira, Carlos, Sofia, and from our side Liam and Priya. Can you hear me okay?
[00:07] Daniel Park: Yep can hear you, thanks Maya.
[00:10] Amira Rahman: All good here.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Great. We'll try to keep this around 45 minutes and then leave time for Q&A. This is a focused demo on structured outputs and tool calling — JSON mode, schemas, guardrails, and a bit of runtime routing. Liam will lead the demo.
[00:26] Liam O'Connor: Thanks Maya. Quick context: Nexus mentioned multi-tenant ingestion where downstream pipelines need deterministic structured events, and you want safe tool invocations for enrichment calls and external lookups — is that still the brief?
[00:38] Daniel Park: Yes that's right. We're ingesting customer logs and creating normalized events; the hard part is consistency and preventing hallucinated lookups to external systems.
[00:47] Carlos Mendes: Also need to keep costs under control; some of our tenants are high-volume.
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: Understood. I'll start by opening the Redwood Console — Demo note: console UI and names sometimes appear as 'Redwood ConThis' in auto transcribes, ignore typos.
[01:05] [01:05] Liam O'Connor: (screen share) Here in the Console you can pick models and choose JSON mode which enforces a schema. I'm going to load a sample schema for your ingestion event — fields like event_type, timestamp, user_id, geo, enrichment.calls array.
[01:25] Amira Rahman: Is the schema a JSON schema draft-07 or do you support openapi types?
[01:30] Liam O'Connor: We accept JSON Schema Draft-07 and a few ergonomic variants; we also let you map to typed contracts in the SDK. There is a schema editor in the Console for quick edits. The enforcement happens at runtime — if the model output doesn't validate the schema we can automatically route to a fallback path or call a repair flow.
[01:46] Sofia Alvarez: For compliance we need an immutable audit trail when a fallback or a repair happens — can you capture that?
[01:52] Priya Singh: Yes, Console captures an audit log entry with the raw model output, validation diff, and the applied correction. Those artifacts are available via the audit API or as an entry in the KMS-backed logs for Private deployments.
[02:07] Daniel Park: How often do repairs trigger? We're worried about cascading costs if repair flows call more tokens or external APIs.
[02:15] Liam O'Connor: Good question. Repair frequency depends on model + schema strictness and sample prompts. In our experience for schema enforced structured data, misvalidation tends to be under 3-7% once prompts and instruction tuning are aligned. We also provide a lightweight deterministic 'repairer' mode that uses a small rules engine to fix predictable formatting issues to avoid re-generation costs.
[02:34] [02:34] Liam O'Connor: Let me demo a tool call pattern — say we want to enrich an event with geo lookup. I'll show a function definition in the Console that maps to an internal service call.
[02:44] [02:44] Liam O'Connor: (typing) Here's a 'geo_lookup' function contract: input ip_address string, output {country, region, city, lat, lon}. When the model decides to call it we surface the call as a structured action and execute the configured integration.
[02:58] Amira Rahman: Is the function executed synchronously on the same serving path? Do you support async callbacks for long-running external actions?
[03:04] Liam O'Connor: Both. For low-latency services we do sync invocations in the runtime. For longer ops we have an async pattern where the model returns a tool-call token and we update the response via an event callback. You can define timeout and retry policies per tool.
[03:18] Carlos Mendes: For multi-tenant, do we have per-tenant secrets for these integrations? We can't have a shared key for all customers.
[03:24] Maya Chen: Yes, in Dedicated and Private you can mount per-tenant credentials and use the vault integrations. In Hosted we support tenant-scoped integration tokens via the Console.
[03:34] Sofia Alvarez: Where are those tokens stored? We need KMS/HSM-backed keys; anything that uses customer-managed keys?
[03:40] Priya Singh: For Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM and you can opt to keep secrets in your vault. For Redwood Hosted we offer KMS integration and bring-your-own-key via a managed HSM option for enterprise accounts.
[03:53] [03:53] Liam O'Connor: Back to JSON mode: I'll run a sample prompt. (runs) The model returns an object that almost matches the schema but the enrichment.calls array is a string instead of an array. Console flags that validation error.
[04:08] [04:08] Liam O'Connor: We have a fallback policy configured — this one attempts a repairer function first (a deterministic normalizer) up to 2 retries, then routes to a canary model with stricter prompt instructions, and finally if all fails it emits a validation error and tags the record for manual review.
[04:25] Daniel Park: Can the fallback route to a cheaper model to reduce cost?
[04:29] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely — routing policies are policy-first: you can route by latency SLO, cost budget, region, or capability. You can do 'prefer cheap' and only promote to high-quality expensive models if lower-tier fails.
[04:41] Amira Rahman: How do you measure cost at token granularity across different fallbacks? We need to forecast unit economics per tenant.
[04:47] Priya Singh: Console + Optimize show token-level cost breakdown per route and per model. Optimize will give suggestions — e.g., try quantized variants, reduce context size to 256 when full context isn't needed, or adjust batching. It will simulate expected cost delta too.
[05:02] [05:02] Carlos Mendes: Do you include KV cache or prefix caching for repeated snippets? We have a lot of repeated onboarding boilerplate in the events.
[05:08] Liam O'Connor: We have prefix/KV caching in the runtime — it's automatic for repeated prefixes and can be pinned per user or per tenant. It reduces tokens and latency.
[05:16] [05:16] Liam O'Connor: (typing) Now I'm switching to the SDK snippet to show function calling. Here the SDK declares the schema, the function contract, and a runtime policy. The call returns a structured action payload which the SDK unwraps and executes.
[05:32] Amira Rahman: Any samples for languages? We use Go and Python heavily.
[05:36] Liam O'Connor: We have SDKs for Python, Node, and a lightweight HTTP wrapper for Go; we'll share the Go example after this call.
[05:44] [05:44] Daniel Park: If we pin a model version, does that include the quantization/compilation profile? We need deterministic latency for a given model pin.
[05:51] Priya Singh: Model pins include model version, compilation profile, and runtime config. For Dedicated we can create a deterministic profile and include it in your SLO.
[05:59] Sofia Alvarez: On data residency — can we keep logs and audit trails inside our VPC and retain them for 7 years?
[06:06] Priya Singh: For Private deployment you can keep logs in your storage and we support custom retention policies. For Hosted accounts we offer log export to your S3/GCS with encryption at rest. Seven years is a long retention but it'd be possible for enterprise compliance upsell.
[06:20] [06:20] Daniel Park: Ok cool. Can you show an example of a 'repair' flow where the model returns a bad date format and how the pipeline fixes it?
[06:27] [06:27] Liam O'Connor: Sure. (runs) Example output: { event_type: "login", timestamp: "14th May, 2027 3:24 PM", user_id: 1132 } — schema expected ISO8601. Console shows the validation diff and executes a repairer that parses the string and rewrites to 2027-05-14T15:24:00Z, then re-validates.
[06:47] [06:47] Liam O'Connor: You can configure if the repaired output is written back as the primary record or if we keep both versions and flag the record. That ties into audit trail requirements.
[06:57] Amira Rahman: That repair step — is that another call to the model or deterministic code?
[07:01] Liam O'Connor: Prefer deterministic when possible — regex parsing, date parsing libraries. We only call the model for complex semantic repairs. That keeps cost lower.
[07:10] [07:10] Daniel Park: Great. A security question: what happens if a model attempts to call an unauthorized function or a function name is spoofed in the payload?
[07:17] Priya Singh: The runtime enforces an allowlist per model and per route. Function contracts are registered and signed; we verify the contract signature before execution. Any mismatch triggers an audit event and the call is blocked.
[07:30] [07:30] Sofia Alvarez: Do you have an example of audit logs output format? We need to ingest into our SIEM.
[07:35] Liam O'Connor: Yes we emit structured audit events (JSON) with event_id, timestamp, raw_model_output, validation_diff, applied_action, and operator. They can be forwarded via syslog, webhook, or pushed to S3.
[07:48] [07:48] Daniel Park: About SSO — we use SAML and our IdP is Okta. Can we get RBAC scoped to environments?
[07:55] Maya Chen: Yes, we integrate with SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC is tenant-aware. For Private you can hook into your internal directory.
[08:05] [08:05] Priya Singh: Also support SCIM group sync to map Okta groups to Console roles.
[08:12] [08:12] Carlos Mendes: Back to pilot — what are the minimum infra commits for a Dedicated pilot? We want something that mimics our volume but is cost contained.
[08:20] Liam O'Connor: For a pilot we usually reserve 1-2 GPU workers (A100/RTX depending on model) for steady-state and configure burst into shared capacity. We'll produce an infra estimate based on your qps and average context.
[08:33] Daniel Park: Any limits on function concurrency? We'll call enrichment APIs that have their own rate limits.
[08:39] Liam O'Connor: You can set per-tool concurrency and global concurrency limits; the runtime will backpressure and queue with priority lanes per tenant.
[08:47] [08:47] Maya Chen: Quick pause — any top risks you want us to address in the SOW?
[08:52] Daniel Park: Security integration complexity, per-tenant cost predictability, and how we handle failure modes where multiple fallbacks still produce invalid outputs.
[08:59] Maya Chen: Good — we'll call that out in the SOW.
[09:02] [09:02] Liam O'Connor: Now switching to Optimize: Optimize looks at historical runs and suggests batching, KV cache policies, and quantization profiles by model. For example, it suggested switching to an 8-bit quantized variant for our 'ingest' workload which dropped token cost by ~30% with minimal quality loss.
[09:21] Amira Rahman: Do you support automated rollout of those config changes? We can't have an automatic drop that hurts data quality.
[09:27] Priya Singh: We support canary rollouts: pick a small tenant subset, run AB, and roll back automatically if quality regressions are detected using the evals tied to your golden prompts.
[09:39] [09:39] Liam O'Connor: Showing the evals tab — here you can associate prompt sets and expected structured outputs, and get regression alerts. You can also attach a guardrail that prevents a rollout if schema error rate increases past a threshold.
[09:53] Daniel Park: That sounds useful. How do you compute quality for structured outputs — token similarity isn't enough.
[09:59] Liam O'Connor: We compute schema-aware comparisons: field-level diffs, numeric tolerances, and include downstream acceptance tests you can plug in. We also have heuristics for semantically-equivalent values.
[10:12] [10:12] Sophia Alvarez: For the pilot, can you anonymize logs before sending to Redwood for diagnostics? We don't want raw PII leaving the environment.
[10:19] Maya Chen: Yes, we can either run diagnostics inside your Private deployment or we can ingest anonymized/sampled logs. We'll include that option in the SOW.
[10:27] [10:27] Liam O'Connor: I'll show an example config file for the runtime routing policy — it's YAML-like in the Console: routes: prefer-cheaper -> fallback to high-quality model on error; retries: 2; repairer: enabled; audit: full.
[10:42] [10:42] Amira Rahman: One practical question — when a function call is made, does Redwood proxy the call or does the SDK call our service directly?
[10:48] Liam O'Connor: Two patterns: proxy via Redwood integration (we call with stored credentials), or the SDK returns the signed action and your platform executes it. Proxy mode is easier for feature parity, but signed action mode keeps control within your network.
[11:02] Carlos Mendes: For network isolation, can the proxy be VPC peered or do you support PrivateLink?
[11:08] Priya Singh: We support VPC peering and PrivateLink for Hosted customers; for Private deployments everything runs in your network.
[11:16] [11:16] Daniel Park: Ok let's talk timeline — we'd like a 2-week pilot and then a 3-month evaluation. Any blockers from your side?
[11:23] Maya Chen: We need a signed pilot SOW, data access parameters, and sample prompts. We'll prepare a SOW template after this call and list required approvals.
[11:31] Daniel Park: Budget is a question; can you give a rough estimate for the pilot costs?
[11:35] Liam O'Connor: We'll provide a ballpark: for the pilot infra estimate and expected token usage we'll send a cost projection. For production we can propose a reserved Dedicated plan to flatten unit costs.
[11:46] [11:46] Sofia Alvarez: Any other customers with similar use cases you can name? We care about references for compliance.
[11:52] Maya Chen: We can share anonymized references in regulated industries; we'll include relevant case studies in the follow-up.
[11:58] [11:58] Amira Rahman: Quick question about model choice: do you recommend mixing open models with Redwood-verified ones?
[12:05] Priya Singh: Often a hybrid works: use cheaper open models for initial parsing and conservative functions, and route to verified variants for high-risk records. Optimize can simulate that mix.
[12:17] [12:17] Liam O'Connor: Wrapping up the demo. I'll attach the Console session and the routing policy snippet to the meeting notes.
[12:24] Daniel Park: Thanks, that was helpful. Couple final clarifications: when you say 'repairer' is that separate from 'moderation' for PII or toxic content?
[12:32] Liam O'Connor: Yes separate. Moderation runs as a pre-step filter; repairer is post-output normalization. Both can be in the pipeline and you can opt to drop records failing moderation entirely.
[12:43] [12:43] Maya Chen: Okay let's recap action items and next steps. Liam — you'll produce the infra estimate and batch/quant profile. I'll send the security pack and SOW. Amira — you'll send prompt sets. Daniel — confirm pilot owners and acceptance criteria.
[12:58] Daniel Park: Sounds good.
[13:01] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[13:03] Carlos Mendes: Not from me.
[13:05] Sofia Alvarez: No, thanks.
[13:07] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts. We'll tentatively schedule pilot kickoff for 2027-05-17 pending approvals.
[13:18] [13:18] Meeting ended.
Notes on transcript quality: some brand names and acronyms mis-transcribed (e.g., "Redwood ConThis" instead of Console, "KV cash" instead of KV cache), occasional filler words removed for readability but pauses preserved.
